title: A 3-item 'done' checklist before you send
source_document: Author Solutions: 10 Tips for Effective Proofreading; Resilience ADHD: ADHD & How to Make Fewer Detail Errors (Zeitlin, May 2026); Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto (cited by Resilience ADHD)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Checklist idea cites Gawande; verify before quoting.
text:
Recognize it when: you send an email, assignment or form and only then notice a missing attachment, a wrong name or a wrong date.
Technique: a short written checklist you run before pressing send, so your memory does not have to do the checking.
How: 1. Write 3 questions that fit your usual slips, for example: Is the attachment there? Is the recipient right? Are dates and numbers right?
2. Keep them in a note, sticky note or pinned message.
3. Before sending, read each question and answer it by looking, not by remembering.
4. Keep it to 3 to 5 items so you actually use it.
Why it helps: ADHD makes holding a mental to-do list unreliable. A visible checklist moves the check outside your head, and checklists are used in high-stakes jobs for the same reason.
Try saying: I do not trust my memory. I trust my three questions.
If it does not work: shorten it to the one error you make most, or let the app set a reminder that shows the list before deadlines.

title: Your eyes skip your own mistakes: change how you read it
source_document: Author Solutions: 10 Tips for Effective Proofreading; Resilience ADHD; ot4adhd and inkwellforge as summarised in the user's research notes
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you re-read your own work three times and still miss typos or missing words.
Technique: make the text look or sound different so your brain reads it fresh instead of auto-filling what it expects.
How: 1. Use text-to-speech or read it aloud slowly.
2. Change the font, zoom in, or switch to dark mode.
3. Print it, or read it from the last sentence to the first.
4. Use a ruler or index card under each line.
5. Pick one of these, not all of them.
Why it helps: After you write something, your brain knows what it meant and reads past errors. A new format breaks that autopilot.
Try saying: Same words, new format. Let me hear it instead of reading it.
If it does not work: if reading aloud is awkward, use text-to-speech with headphones, or ask one person to read it to you.

title: Do not write and proofread in the same sitting
source_document: Author Solutions; Resilience ADHD (small batches, leave time at the end); user's research summary
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you finish writing and immediately start checking, or you rush to send because the deadline is close.
Technique: treat drafting and checking as two separate jobs with a break between them, and check in small pieces.
How: 1. Stop writing when the draft is done.
2. Take a break of 5 to 15 minutes, or longer for important work.
3. Check one paragraph or one small batch at a time rather than the whole document.
4. Check for one type of error per pass (spelling first, then numbers, then tone).
5. Plan the check into your schedule so it is not squeezed out by the deadline.
Why it helps: Checking a small piece with fresh eyes is easier on attention than scanning a long document once. Time pressure is the usual reason checking gets skipped.
Try saying: Draft now, check later. They are two different jobs.
If it does not work: set a timer for the break and a second timer for the check so both actually happen.

title: Let tools do the first pass, then you do the last
source_document: Resilience ADHD (use spellcheck/grammar/AI but keep your brain on); Author Solutions (use spellcheck but do not trust it); user's research summary
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you rely on spellcheck and still send mistakes, or you skip checking because a tool exists.
Technique: use a tool for the first sweep, then do a short human check for what tools miss.
How: 1. Run spellcheck or a grammar tool.
2. If you use an AI helper, ask it only to list problems, for example: List any typos, missing words, or tone issues without rewriting my text.
3. Then do one pass yourself for names, dates, numbers and whether it says what you meant.
4. Remember that spellcheck accepts real words in the wrong place.
Why it helps: Tools catch what is mechanical and free your attention for what only you can judge. Asking for a list, not a rewrite, keeps your own voice and keeps you in the loop.
Try saying: Tool first, me second.
If it does not work: if you tend to accept every suggestion without looking, ask for the list and fix each item by hand.

title: A second pair of eyes and an undo-send buffer
source_document: Resilience ADHD (checks and balances); Author Solutions (have someone else read it); user's research summary
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: a mistake only gets caught after it reaches your boss, teacher or client, or you feel you cannot catch your own errors.
Technique: build a second check outside yourself: a reviewer, and a short delay before anything leaves your outbox.
How: 1. For important work, ask a friend, colleague or classmate to scan it for 2 minutes.
2. Tell them what to look for (numbers, names, missing words), not just 'check it'.
3. Turn on undo send with a delay of about 30 seconds in your email app.
4. If nobody is available, do the 2-minute check with a body double on a call.
Why it helps: Other people do not auto-correct your text in their head. A delay gives you a last chance to notice the slip.
Try saying: Could you give this two minutes and tell me if any number or name looks off?
If it does not work: if asking feels embarrassing, frame it as a team habit: I check others' work and they check mine.

title: Know your own error pattern
source_document: Author Solutions (know your Achilles' heels); Resilience ADHD (measure your error rate)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you feel you are just careless, but the same kinds of mistakes keep repeating.
Technique: track what your mistakes actually are so your checklist targets them.
How: 1. For one or two weeks, note each mistake in a short list (wrong date, missing word, wrong recipient).
2. Count them and see which type appears most.
3. Put that one type at the top of your checklist.
4. Look again after two weeks to see if it dropped.
Why it helps: Most people repeat a small set of errors. Naming yours turns 'I am careless' into 'I mix up dates', which is fixable.
Try saying: My mistakes have a pattern, and a pattern can be fixed.
If it does not work: if logging feels heavy, just keep a note titled 'my usual slips' and add to it when one happens.

title: Checking physical actions (stove, door, lights) without worrying
source_document: Manas synthesis based on implementation intentions (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006) and the checklist idea in Resilience ADHD
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Application to physical checks is a Manas synthesis. Verify citations.
text:
Recognize it when: you leave the house unsure you turned off the stove or locked the door, or you realise you did something on autopilot.
Technique: pair the action with one deliberate check at the moment you do it, so there is a memory to rely on.
How: 1. Say what you are doing out loud as you do it: Stove off. Door locked.
2. Or take a quick photo of the switch or lock as proof.
3. Put a small if-then rule on it: If I turn the key, then I say 'locked' and touch the handle once.
4. Use the same routine every time so it becomes automatic.
Why it helps: ADHD makes autopilot actions leave no memory trace. A spoken word or photo creates one, so you can check the record instead of worrying.
Try saying: I checked it already. I have the photo.
If it does not work: if worry about checking becomes constant or distressing, mention it to a clinician, since repeated checking can also be a separate problem.

title: The 4 R's: Recognize, Respond, Reflect, Reframe
source_document: ADDA (add.org): Rejection Sensitivity, Managing Feelings of Overwhelm and Rejection as an Adult with ADHD (Gordon, updated Nov 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. RSD is not a DSM-5 diagnosis; rejection sensitivity is backed by research.
text:
Recognize it when: a short text, a pause in a conversation or small feedback lands like a punch and you feel flooded.
Technique: the 4 R's: Recognize your intensity, Respond to match it, Reflect on the story, Reframe with other explanations.
How: 1. Recognize: check your body (flushed face, clenched stomach or fists). The more intense you are, the less clearly you think, so it is not the time to argue or ask for things.
2. Respond: green (calm): do daily calming habits. Yellow (rising): unclench your jaw, slow your breathing, take a short walk. Red (flooded): move your body (jog, jumping jacks, cuddle a pet) to burn off the surge.
3. Reflect: What story am I telling myself? What evidence is there? What else could it be?
4. Reframe: write one or two other reasons for their reply (busy, tired, different preference).
Why it helps: It matches the tool to how intense you are, and only asks you to think once your body has settled.
Try saying: Where am I on green, yellow or red? Let me match my tool to that.
If it does not work: practise the yellow tools when calm so they are ready when you are flooded.

title: Name the wave and hold your reply
source_document: Neurodiverse Counseling (Mansouri, LICSW): Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria and ADHD, How to Cope; user's research summary (name it to tame it)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Rule of 'one hour' is a suggestion from the source, not a tested number.
text:
Recognize it when: you feel crushed and want to send a reply, defend yourself, or cancel plans right now.
Technique: label the feeling, delay the reply, and use your body to settle.
How: 1. Say it: This is an RSD wave. It feels huge, and it will pass.
2. Do not reply to a charged message for about an hour.
3. Press your feet into the floor, put a hand on your chest, take three slow breaths with a longer exhale.
4. Come back and ask: What do I actually know, and what am I filling in?
Why it helps: Naming the emotion engages the thinking part of the brain and reminds you the feeling is a reaction moving through you, not a fact about your worth. A short delay lets the intensity drop.
Try saying: This is just RSD talking, not an actual emergency.
If it does not work: if you cannot wait, write the reply in your notes app and send nothing yet.

title: Build a counter-evidence folder
source_document: User's research summary of RSD coping sources (CBT/REBT style); Unlock Psychology: Coping With Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Based on CBT-style cognitive restructuring.
text:
Recognize it when: one criticism or bad moment feels like proof that you are bad at everything, and good feedback is forgotten.
Technique: keep a folder of real evidence against that story and read it when the spiral starts.
How: 1. Create a note or folder titled Evidence.
2. Each time someone thanks you, praises your work, or a plan went well, save it (screenshot or one line).
3. When you spiral, ask: What happened? Then open the folder and read three items.
4. For a mind-reading thought, write 2 to 3 other explanations next to it.
Why it helps: The ADHD brain sticks to negatives. Writing down positives stores them where you can find them on a bad day.
Try saying: One hard moment is data, not a verdict.
If it does not work: start with just one saved item this week.

title: Feedback is about the task, not your worth
source_document: Neurodiverse Counseling (Mansouri); ADDA 4 R's; user's research summary (constructive criticism about task, not worth)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: a manager, teacher or friend gave feedback and you heard 'I am not good enough', or you now avoid asking for feedback.
Technique: split the feedback into what to change in the work and what your feelings say about you.
How: 1. Write the feedback in one neutral sentence (The report needs a clearer summary).
2. Draw two columns: About the task / About me. Only the first column came from them.
3. Pick one small change you can make.
4. Ask one clarifying question if you are unsure what they meant.
5. If you want to avoid asking for feedback, ask for just one thing: What is one thing to improve?
Why it helps: When feedback feels like worth being judged, you either defend or avoid. Splitting it makes the useful part easy to act on.
Try saying: This is about the report. I am more than the report.
If it does not work: if criticism feels personal every time, a therapist (CBT or compassion-focused) can help.

title: When RSD hits hardest: tired, hungry, overloaded
source_document: Neurodiverse Counseling (Mansouri): track your patterns
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you are more easily hurt on some days than others and cannot tell why.
Technique: track what state you were in when it hit, then plan around those states.
How: 1. After a strong reaction, note: time, how tired or hungry you were, who or what set it off.
2. Look for patterns after a week or two.
3. On those risky days, avoid hard conversations and send fewer replies.
4. Eat, sleep and take breaks before difficult talks.
Why it helps: Sensitivity rises with tiredness, hunger and overstimulation. Knowing this replaces self-blame with planning.
Try saying: Part of this is that I am tired. I will revisit it after I eat and rest.
If it does not work: if no pattern shows up, ask a trusted person what they notice.

title: What if they really are upset with me?
source_document: ADDA: What if People Really Don't Want to Play with You; Neurodiverse Counseling (safe connections)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you checked the facts and it does seem someone is annoyed or rejected you.
Technique: separate what you control (your response, who you spend time with) from what you cannot (how others feel).
How: 1. Name what is real: They may be upset, and that is allowed to hurt.
2. Decide one calm action: ask a clear question, apologise once if you owe it, or let it be.
3. Do not re-send or over-explain.
4. Spend time with someone who accepts you.
Why it helps: Rejection that is real still hurts, but a calm response is under your control. Safe connections soften the impact over time.
Try saying: I cannot control how they feel. I can control how I respond.
If it does not work: if it keeps happening across relationships, a therapist can help find the pattern.

title: Why you blurt or interrupt (and why it is not rudeness)
source_document: Life Skills Advocate: 14 Tips for Overcoming Interrupting with ADHD (Pierce); ScienceWorks on interrupting/blurting
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you speak over people or blurt out thoughts and then feel bad.
Technique: understand the likely reasons, then pick one small habit instead of trying to fix everything.
How: 1. Common reasons: thoughts feel urgent and slip away if not said; fast thinking and speaking; boredom or overwhelm in long talks; distraction pulling attention away.
2. Pick one cause that fits you.
3. Choose one habit from the others (notes, count, question).
Why it helps: Knowing why it happens helps you aim at the right fix, and lowers shame, which makes you more likely to keep trying.
Try saying: I interrupt because ideas feel urgent. I can give them somewhere to go.
If it does not work: if it harms work or relationships, executive-function coaching or a clinician can help.

title: Write the thought down instead of saying it
source_document: Life Skills Advocate (take notes; post reminders)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you fear forgetting your point, so you jump in before the other person finishes.
Technique: keep a pen or note open and jot a few keywords so the thought is saved.
How: 1. Keep a notepad or phone note open in meetings and chats.
2. When a thought comes, write 2 or 3 words.
3. Wait until the person finishes, then use the note to speak.
4. Notes also signal to your brain: listening time.
Why it helps: The urge to interrupt is often fear of losing the idea. A written note removes that fear.
Try saying: My point is saved. I can wait.
If it does not work: if writing distracts you, use a single keyword per thought.

title: Count and breathe before you speak
source_document: Life Skills Advocate (timeouts, deep breathing); Zylowska, Mindfulness Prescription for Adult ADHD (cited by source)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you start talking as soon as someone pauses, and you cut them off.
Technique: a silent count or one breath before replying.
How: 1. When they stop, breathe in once, or count silently to 3 to 10.
2. Watch for cues (they look at you, their tone drops, their hands settle).
3. If someone else starts, let them.
4. Practise first with a low-stakes chat or a friend.
Why it helps: A tiny delay creates space between impulse and speech, and gives quieter people room to join.
Try saying: I will take one breath first.
If it does not work: count to 3 only if 10 feels too long.

title: If you do interrupt: apologise briefly and hand the floor back
source_document: Life Skills Advocate (ask permission, apologise, be honest, ask questions)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you caught yourself mid-interruption, or you often get a reaction like 'let me finish'.
Technique: a short repair plus a question to bring them back in.
How: 1. Stop and say: Sorry, go ahead.
2. Or ask: Can I add something? or Can I share a thought when you are done?
3. Ask a question about what they said instead of competing.
4. If it was a pattern, be honest once: My brain jumps in sometimes. Tell me if I do.
Why it helps: A quick, calm repair keeps trust and shows you were listening. A long apology adds shame without helping.
Try saying: Sorry, go ahead. I want to hear the rest.
If it does not work: ask a friend to give you a quiet signal when you start to jump in.

title: Rehearse and track how often you interrupt
source_document: Life Skills Advocate (be aware of frequency, rehearse, practise with a friend)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you want to improve but do not know where to start.
Technique: measure first, then rehearse one strategy.
How: 1. In one conversation, count how many times you interrupt.
2. Choose one strategy (note, count, question).
3. Rehearse in your head before the next meeting, or practise with a friend.
4. Count again next week.
Why it helps: A number makes progress visible, which is motivating, and rehearsal makes the habit easier to use under pressure.
Try saying: I interrupted 5 times last week. I will aim for 3.
If it does not work: track just one meeting a week.

title: Cleaning a room: four piles and a 'not sure' box
source_document: Healthline: ADHD and messy; Neural Revolution: ADHD organization; user's research notes (room reset)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: your room is messy and every item raises a decision: keep, throw, move?
Technique: sort into four piles and put unsure items in a dated box.
How: 1. Make four spots: Keep, Discard, Move to another room, Unsure.
2. Pick up one item at a time and put it in a pile within 5 seconds.
3. Put every Unsure item in one box, write the date, and seal it.
4. If you do not open it for 30 days, donate or throw it away.
Why it helps: Quick sorting avoids long decisions, and the box removes the pressure to decide now.
Try saying: I do not have to decide now. It goes in the Unsure box.
If it does not work: if even four piles is too much, start with just trash.

title: The go-back basket for things that belong elsewhere
source_document: Neural Revolution: ADHD organization; user's research notes
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you carry things around the house, put them down anywhere, and the clutter spreads.
Technique: a basket near the door or the bottom of the stairs for misplaced items.
How: 1. Put a basket where you pass often.
2. Drop anything that belongs in another room into it.
3. Empty it once a day or when it is full, putting each item back.
4. Pair it with something you already do, such as after dinner.
Why it helps: It removes the need to return each item immediately, which is the step that usually breaks down.
Try saying: I do not need to walk it back now. It goes in the basket.
If it does not work: empty it only twice a week at first.

title: Make tidy-up easy: open bins, clear shelves, hamper where you drop clothes
source_document: ADDitude: No More Messy House; Neural Revolution; Private Therapy Clinic: Overcoming ADHD Disorganisation; user's research notes
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: closed drawers hide things until you forget them, or putting things away takes too many steps.
Technique: set up storage to match your habits and show what you own.
How: 1. Use clear bins, open shelves or hanging baskets so you can see items.
2. Put the hamper where you actually drop clothes.
3. Use open-top bins instead of lids.
4. Give each item one home and label it with a word or picture.
Why it helps: Out of sight is often out of mind with ADHD. Fewer steps means the habit is more likely to happen.
Try saying: If putting it away takes one step, I will do it.
If it does not work: change one spot at a time.

title: 5-10 minute burst and a body double for tidying
source_document: ADDitude: messy room and executive function; user's research notes; Healthline
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: the room feels too big to start, or you start and burn out.
Technique: short timed bursts with music, and company if possible.
How: 1. Set a timer for 5 to 10 minutes and play one upbeat song.
2. Clear only one zone or one surface.
3. Stop when the timer ends, even if it feels unfinished.
4. Invite a friend to sit in the room, or video call while you tidy.
Why it helps: A short, fixed end makes starting easy, and company lowers the barrier to begin.
Try saying: Just one song. Then I can stop.
If it does not work: shrink to 2 minutes and pick up only the trash.

title: Zones and 'a home for everything'
source_document: Source: ADHD & Organization: Systems for Adults (functional zones, point of performance, everything has a home)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: things get lost because they are stored far from where you use them.
Technique: store things at the point of use and group by activity zone.
How: 1. Notice where you use an item (keys by the door, charger by the bed).
2. Put its home there.
3. Create zones: work, hygiene, relax.
4. Use a weekly 10-minute reset at a set time.
Why it helps: Items put near where they are used need less effort, and a fixed home reduces searching.
Try saying: Where do I use this? That is where it lives.
If it does not work: start with the three items you lose most.

title: Too many options: choose good enough from 2 or 3
source_document: Marla Cummins: solution for ADHD adults overwhelmed by choices; AMFM blog; Ready Health: ADHD and decision fatigue (Sept 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Satisficing idea from Herbert Simon; Ready Health notes decision fatigue is not an ADHD symptom requirement.
text:
Recognize it when: a menu, shop aisle or list of tasks gives you too many options and you freeze.
Technique: set a good-enough standard and cut the options to 2 or 3.
How: 1. Decide what counts as good enough (under 20 minutes, under a set price).
2. Remove options that fail the filter.
3. Compare at most 2 or 3 of what is left.
4. Pick, then stop looking.
Why it helps: Fewer options reduce load on working memory. Good enough saves energy for choices that matter.
Try saying: Good enough is a decision.
If it does not work: ask someone to pick for you once, then stop asking.

title: Get the options out of your head: write two criteria
source_document: AMFM blog; ADHD Coaching Works: ADHD decision paralysis (Sept 2026); Marla Cummins
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: you keep going around in circles on the same decision.
Technique: put the options on paper and score them on two criteria.
How: 1. Write the decision at the top.
2. List the options.
3. Choose two things that matter most (cost, time, how you feel).
4. Score each option 1 to 5 and add up.
5. Choose the highest and decide if it can be changed later.
Why it helps: Writing frees working memory, and two criteria stops endless comparing.
Try saying: Two criteria, one pick, and I can adjust later.
If it does not work: if scores tie, flip a coin and notice which result you hope for.

title: Big decisions (two job offers, a move): a calm structure
source_document: Manas synthesis from AMFM time-boxing, 10-10-10 and decision criteria; Ready Health decision fatigue article
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited. Manas synthesis, not a single source.
text:
Recognize it when: you have a major choice such as two job offers and you cannot stop thinking about it.
Technique: set a deadline, pick three criteria, gather facts once, and decide with a person you trust.
How: 1. Set a decision date, no later than a week or two.
2. Choose 3 criteria (pay, growth, people).
3. Write what you actually know about each option, and the questions you still need to ask.
4. Ask the recruiter or a trusted person those questions once.
5. Score, and run the 10-10-10 check.
6. Decide at the deadline, even if not perfect.
Why it helps: A deadline and a few criteria stop endless looping. Most big choices have no perfect answer, only a good fit.
Try saying: I will decide by Friday with what I know.
If it does not work: if the pressure is intense, calm your body first and talk it through with someone.

title: The burnt toast idea (a popular reframe, not research)
source_document: Popular social-media framing; coverage by Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials, Refinery29 and others
source_citation: Viral anecdote. Not a research-based theory. Origin is attributed to a popular story, not studies. Verify before citing as science.
text:
Recognize it when: a small setback (a delay, a mistake, a missed bus) is making you feel the day is ruined.
Technique: the burnt toast story: a small annoyance may have redirected you, so you can look for the possible upside without forcing positivity.
How: 1. Say the facts: I missed it or I was delayed.
2. Say the story: sometimes small setbacks change what happens next.
3. Ask: Is there any possible upside, or is there a next step I can take?
4. If not, accept that it was just a bad moment.
5. Say clearly that this is a popular reframe, not proof.
Why it helps: It gives your brain another story to hold besides disaster, which may lower distress. The effect has not been studied as a theory.
Try saying: This might be my burnt toast moment. Or it might just be toast. Either way I can take the next step.
If it does not work: if a setback feels serious, do not force a bright side. Skip the reframe and use a grounding step.

title: The 90-second wave (popular idea, treat as approximate)
source_document: Popularised from Jill Bolte Taylor, My Stroke of Insight; discussed in Shortform and other popular summaries
source_citation: Popular simplification. The claim that a feeling lasts 90 seconds is not established as a rule for all emotions, and rumination can restart it. Use as a gentle guide.
text:
Recognize it when: an emotion hits hard and you want to act before it passes.
Technique: treat the first surge as a wave that rises and falls, and wait through it without feeding it.
How: 1. Notice the wave: where in your body?
2. Breathe slowly for about a minute or two.
3. Do not replay the story while you wait.
4. If it returns, that is usually the replay, so return to breathing.
5. Then decide what to do.
Why it helps: It makes a strong feeling feel temporary and gives a small task for the first minute. Exact timing varies.
Try saying: Let me ride this wave for a minute before I choose.
If it does not work: if the feeling is still huge after several minutes, it may need a longer break, movement or a trusted person.

title: The habit loop: cue, craving, response, reward
source_document: James Clear, Atomic Habits (four stages); Duhigg, The Power of Habit (cue, routine, reward); Lally et al. (2010)
source_citation: Atomic Habits is a popular book that builds on habit research. Lally et al. (2010) found habit formation took about 66 days on average with wide variation. Verify before citing.
text:
Recognize it when: you want a new habit to stick, or you want to change an old one.
Technique: start from the cue and design all four stages: cue, craving, response, reward.
How: 1. Cue: tie it to something you already do or a clear time and place.
2. Craving: make it appealing (music, a drink, a small treat).
3. Response: make it tiny and easy.
4. Reward: end with something satisfying (tick on a tracker, a small treat).
5. To drop a bad habit, change the cue, remove the craving, add friction or change the reward.
Why it helps: Most habits fail at the cue or the reward step. Designing each stage shows where yours breaks.
Try saying: What is my cue? What is my reward?
If it does not work: if you miss a day, restart the next day. Missing once does not undo the habit.

title: Invictus: the poem Nelson Mandela reportedly recited in prison
source_document: William Ernest Henley, Invictus (1888, public domain); widely reported that Nelson Mandela drew strength from it on Robben Island
source_citation: Public domain poem. Mandela's connection is widely documented, but check the specific lines used before quoting more than a phrase.
text:
Recognize it when: someone feels powerless, ashamed or beaten down after a setback or criticism.
Technique: offer a short, well-sourced line that shows that dignity is possible under pressure.
How: 1. Say the context in one sentence: Henley wrote Invictus after serious illness and surgery, and Nelson Mandela reportedly recited it during his years in prison.
2. Offer one line: I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul.
3. Link it to their situation: The criticism does not decide who you are.
4. Then offer one concrete next step.
Why it helps: A line with real history behind it feels earned, and it points to choice rather than empty cheering.
Try saying: People have stood in far harder places and held on to this line. You get to choose your next step.
If it does not work: if the person is in distress, skip the poem and ask how they are doing first.

title: The man in the arena: fear of criticism
source_document: Theodore Roosevelt, Citizenship in a Republic (Sorbonne, April 1910), public domain
source_citation: Public domain speech. Quote only short phrases; check the exact wording against the speech text before quoting.
text:
Recognize it when: fear of being judged is stopping you from sharing, trying or speaking up.
Technique: remind them that the person who tries matters more than the critics watching.
How: 1. Give context: Theodore Roosevelt gave this speech in Paris in 1910.
2. Offer the idea (paraphrase): credit belongs to the person who is actually in the arena, not the critic.
3. Say: you do not have to be flawless, only willing to try.
4. Suggest a small visible step (share the draft, ask the question).
Why it helps: It puts critics in perspective and values effort over perfection.
Try saying: Critics watch. You are doing. That counts for more.
If it does not work: if the fear feels overwhelming, break the step even smaller.

title: Ideas from The Mountain Is You and The Courage to Be Disliked (paraphrased)
source_document: Brianna Wiest, The Mountain Is You (2020); Kishimi & Koga, The Courage to Be Disliked (2013/2018 English)
source_citation: Paraphrases of the books' central ideas, not quotes. These books are copyrighted. Do not reproduce passages. Verify framing.
text:
Recognize it when: someone feels they are the obstacle, or they are afraid of what people think.
Technique: use a book's idea as a lens, in plain words, with the title and author named.
How: 1. The Mountain Is You: self-sabotage often shows up as a way of protecting yourself, so the work is understanding the pattern kindly rather than hating yourself.
2. The Courage to Be Disliked: the book draws on Adlerian psychology and argues that you cannot control others' judgments, and that separating your tasks from theirs brings freedom.
3. Offer one: Notice what you are protecting, or ask whose task this is.
4. Suggest one small action.
Why it helps: A well-known framework gives people language for their patterns and makes self-reflection feel less lonely.
Try saying: What if the thing getting in the way is trying to protect you? What would you do if disapproval were not the deciding factor?
If it does not work: if the person wants exact quotes, they should read the book and cite it.

title: Keep a list of your usual mistakes and search for them with Ctrl+F
source_document: Author Solutions: 10 Tips for Effective Proofreading (know your own error patterns); user's research notes
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Ctrl+F step is a practical extension of the error-pattern tip.
text:
Recognize it when: you keep making the same slips (wrong names, there/their, double spaces, a date format) and miss them when rereading.
Technique: write your own error list once, then search the document for each item before you send.
How: 1. Keep a note called My usual slips with 5 to 10 items (for example: their/there, double spaces, wrong name spelling, 'form' vs 'from').
2. When you finish writing, press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on Mac) and search each item one at a time.
3. Fix each match, then tick it off.
4. Add a new item whenever someone catches a mistake.
5. As a last pass, read the text backward, one sentence at a time.
Why it helps: Searching is mechanical, so it does not depend on attention. Reading backward breaks the habit of auto-filling what you meant.
Try saying: My mistakes repeat, so I can search for them.
If it does not work: start with the top 3 items and add one a week.

title: The mirror room idea: you drift toward your surroundings
source_document: User-supplied popular framing; origin not verified
source_citation: User-supplied metaphor, source unverified. Not a research theory. Related popular idea: you are shaped by the people and habits around you.
text:
Recognize it when: you feel stuck with moods, habits or self-talk that came from the people or places around you, or you wonder why you feel different around different people.
Technique: treat your surroundings like a mirror room: what you spend time around reflects back at you, so you can change the reflection by changing what is in the room.
How: 1. Notice one person or place that leaves you drained and one that leaves you lighter.
2. Ask: what do I take on from each (tone, habits, ways of talking about myself)?
3. Add one more of what helps (a friend, a routine, a space).
4. Limit one thing that does not, without cutting anyone off.
5. Say clearly it is a metaphor, not a scientific rule.
Why it helps: It makes the environment a lever you can adjust, which is easier than changing yourself by force. It also supports reaching for safe connections.
Try saying: What is reflecting back at me in this room? What do I want in it?
If it does not work: if you cannot change the room, change how much time you spend in it, or add one supportive person.

title: The unfinished room idea: what people leave behind in your mind
source_document: User-supplied popular framing; origin not verified
source_citation: User-supplied metaphor, source unverified. Not a research theory. Related real ideas: rumination and unresolved feelings about people. If grief or trauma, suggest a clinician.
text:
Recognize it when: someone left your life (breakup, friendship, loss, a person who hurt you) and you keep thinking about them, or you feel something is left undone.
Technique: picture the person as a room in your mind that they left unfinished; you choose whether to keep living in the mess or to tidy and rearrange it.
How: 1. Name what is left in the room: a memory, an unsaid thing, a feeling.
2. Decide what you keep (a good memory, a lesson) and what you put away.
3. Do one small tidying act: write the unsent letter, say what you needed to say in a note, or let yourself feel it for 10 minutes.
4. Rearrange the room with something new (a habit, a plan, a friend).
5. If it still hurts a lot, talk with someone you trust or a therapist.
Why it helps: It gives you a sense of agency over rumination. Closure is something you build, not something you wait for.
Try saying: I cannot take the room away, but I can clean and rearrange it.
If it does not work: if the feeling is heavy or grief-like and does not ease, a therapist can help. This metaphor is a framing, not treatment.

title: Thinking by Walter D. Wintle: a poem used in Think and Grow Rich
source_document: Walter D. Wintle, Thinking (published 1905, Unity Tract Society; public domain). Included without an author's name in the 1937 edition of Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich
source_citation: Poem is public domain (1905). The line 'If you think you are beaten, you are' is the opening. Napoleon Hill's book is copyrighted and not research-based; do not quote it.
text:
Recognize it when: someone has decided in advance that they cannot do something or they have already been beaten.
Technique: offer one line from a public-domain poem with its history, then turn it into one small step.
How: 1. Context: Walter D. Wintle's poem Thinking appeared in 1905, and Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich later included it.
2. Line: If you think you are beaten, you are.
3. Turn it: what you believe shapes whether you try. Do not promise it guarantees success.
4. Ask for one small step: What is one thing you can try today?
Why it helps: A short, real line with history can shift a belief. Pairing it with one step keeps it practical.
Try saying: A line from an old poem says if you think you are beaten, you are. Let us test that belief with one small step.
If it does not work: skip it if the person is grieving or in crisis. Ask how they are first.

title: Ideas from Think and Grow Rich (paraphrased, popular not scientific)
source_document: Napoleon Hill, Think and Grow Rich (1937); popular summaries
source_citation: Motivational classic, not evidence-based. Paraphrase only; do not quote. Claims about wealth and the subconscious are not scientifically established. Confirm this is the book the user means.
text:
Recognize it when: someone wants a goal (money, career, study) but feels unmotivated or unclear.
Technique: borrow the book's practical frames in plain words: a definite goal, a written plan, and daily repetition.
How: 1. State one specific goal and a date.
2. Write what you will do each day toward it.
3. Read it aloud morning and night (the book calls this autosuggestion; it is a repetition habit, not magic).
4. Surround yourself with a few people who help you.
5. Say clearly: this is a popular motivational frame, not research.
Why it helps: A clear goal plus repetition matches goal-setting and implementation-intention research (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006) far better than the book's claims about the subconscious.
Try saying: Pick one clear goal. Write it down. Repeat it daily. Then take the next step.
If it does not work: if you want evidence, use if-then plans or the habit loop instead.
